extracted.intended_audience: business school students, instructors, researchers and practitioners in aviation safety, engineering management, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: A teaching case analyzing the design, certification, corporate, and regulatory causes of the Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashes and the subsequent oversight, remediation, and organizational lessons for aviation safety and engineering management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy for critical systems / avoid single points of failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineers build redundancy into systems to avoid 'single points of failure' in which the failure of a single component causes an accident or stops the system from operating. The revised MCAS depended only on AOA data from a single sensor (alternating after each flight), creating a single point-of-failure hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design critical flight-control functions to use redundant, independent sensors (e.g., Airbus uses three AOA sensors). Do not allow a single sensor failure to trigger automatic control actions that can drive the aircraft toward unsafe states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make safety-critical cockpit alerts and indicators standard, not optional
rubrics_metrics.description: The AOA indicator and the AOA DISAGREE alert were not standard equipment on the 737 MAX but offered as optional add-ons; MCAS relied on a single sensor so aircraft without the optional disagree alert would not directly report sensor problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat instrumentation and disagree/warning alerts tied to safety-critical systems as standard equipment. Avoid pushing safety features behind optional packages that airlines may decline for cost reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely reporting and documentation of design changes during certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing modified MCAS (increased stabilizer authority, removed G-force requirement) during testing but did not submit certification documents detailing the change; FAA flight test personnel were aware but key certification engineers were not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit all substantive design changes and associated formal safety risk assessments to regulators promptly during certification. Ensure documentation is complete and reaches the personnel responsible for approval and training decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess system-level safety risks appropriately (classify catastrophic risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing's safety analysis did not assess system-level safety risks as catastrophic; as a result, MCAS was designed to rely on data from a single sensor rather than including redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct system-level hazard analyses and classify risks appropriately (including catastrophic). Where catastrophic outcomes are plausible, adopt design mitigations (redundancy, degraded-mode protections) commensurate with that classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory review must scrutinize novel flight-control software rather than accept 'minor modification' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing positioned MCAS as a modification to existing speed trim functionality and argued differences were not significant; FAA therefore did not emphasize MCAS in certification, limiting detailed review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators should independently evaluate whether new or modified flight-control functions are truly minor; novel software that can change handling characteristics should receive detailed scrutiny rather than being treated as an incremental change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate pilot training, including simulator training when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing initially proposed no simulator training for MAX pilots, later recommended simulator training; FAA later issued policy memos about pilot training for the 737-8 and 737-9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require and provide appropriate pilot training that covers new automated behaviors and failure modes; when automatic systems can induce nonstandard handling, simulator-based training should be mandated rather than optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for process safety (intrinsic system safety) to reduce human error reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety experts argued that many human errors result from poorly designed equipment and systems; designers should focus on 'process safety'—designing intrinsically safe systems that minimize opportunities for and consequences of human error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize design changes that reduce the chance of operator error and minimize the consequences when errors occur (e.g., provide fail-safe modes, automatic protections that degrade safely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an organizational culture that allows and rewards reporting safety concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Before cultural changes, Boeing engineers could raise safety concerns even if it held up progress. After organizational shifts (e.g., post-merger), employees reported a culture of fear where dissent was punished; internal communications show employees expressed disdain for management undermining quality and safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster open channels for engineers, inspectors, and test pilots to raise safety issues without retaliation. Ensure management encourages candid reporting and acts on substantive concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid compressed schedules and resource pressures that undermine quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The 737 MAX program operated on a compressed timeline—engineers were pushed to produce work at roughly double the normal pace; technicians reported sloppy blueprints and instructions deferred to 'cleaned up later'—creating conditions that did not reward people willing to buck managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate realistic schedules and adequate resources for engineering, testing, documentation, and supplier oversight. Recognize that excessive schedule pressure increases error rates and reduces opportunities to fix defects before production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure supply-chain quality, calibration, and complete maintenance documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A sensor supplied second-hand by a Florida company was not calibrated correctly and Lion Air maintenance logs were missing pages; the faulty sensor fed incorrect information to MCAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement strict supplier oversight, incoming inspection, calibration procedures, and rigorous maintenance record-keeping. Treat critical sensor sourcing and installation as key safety controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equip systems to automatically detect and report sensor disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers created a cockpit display for AOA readings and an 'AOA DISAGREE' alert if the two sensors differed, but the disagree alert relied on the AOA indicator option being purchased; without it, crews would not be alerted automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple sensors exist, enable automatic cross-checks and visible, reliable alerts that do not depend on optional equipment choices. Alerts should be clear and actionable to flight crews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flight test and pilot feedback fully and keep test pilots informed of changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark Forkner, chief technical pilot for the 737 MAX, was apparently not informed about some MCAS changes but discovered them in the flight simulator and complained; flight-test personnel reported being pressed to approve many open design review issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate test pilots and flight-test crews into iterative design discussions; ensure they are informed of changes and their feedback is incorporated into risk assessments and pilot procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory independence and strong oversight structures
rubrics_metrics.description: The DOT Inspector General identified limitations in FAA guidance/processes that impacted certification, including communication gaps, management and oversight weaknesses, and processes that did not ensure FAA personnel are adequately independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regulatory structures and processes that preserve technical independence, robust communication, and clear accountability so oversight is effective even when industry seeks fast-tracked approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent communication with airlines, pilots, and the public about safety features and changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing 'didn't tell Southwest and other carriers when they began flying its 737 MAX jets that a safety feature found on earlier models that warns pilots about malfunctioning sensors had been deactivated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose materially relevant changes to system behavior, optional equipment impacts, and safety-related design choices to operators, regulators, and where appropriate, the public. Do not conceal deactivations or downgrades of prior safety functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify design decisions and corporate incentives to prioritize safety over short-term commercial goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions (e.g., pursue faster-to-market update of 737 rather than a new airplane) were driven by commercial pressure to beat Airbus; management changes emphasized running the company 'like a business' and focused on shareholder value which some argue shifted priorities away from engineering-led safety culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align corporate incentives, governance, and board oversight to ensure safety-critical engineering judgments are not overridden by short-term commercial pressures. Executive accountability and safety governance should be explicit and enforced.
